claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding undergo Cr–Zr interdiffusion under accident-relevant high-temperature conditions.
Placing an Al2O3 interlayer between Cr and zirconium alloy will reduce Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The Al2O3 interlayer will improve Cr-coating durability in both subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
The proposed intervention is deposition of a thin, adherent Al2O3 layer at the Cr/Zr interface.
The operative structural mediator is a continuous, chemically stable Al2O3 interfacial layer.
Al2O3 acts as a diffusion barrier to Cr and Zr atoms at the coating/substrate interface.
Limiting Cr and Zr transport will prevent or slow formation of detrimental Cr–Zr intermetallic phases.
Al2O3 can provide resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
The interlayer will maintain the oxidation and corrosion resistance of Cr in both subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
The modified coating will have a thinner oxide scale than the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
The modified coating will show less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than the unmodified baseline.
The modified coating will retain better overall coating integrity than the unmodified baseline.
Elemental Cr coatings are protective in the two service regimes but can fail prematurely because of high-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The applicable subcritical-water condition is approximately 300°C in pressurized water.
The applicable accident condition is steam at approximately 900–1000°C for a short duration.
The intervention remains effective only while the Al2O3 layer remains adherent and intact.
Temperatures beyond the interlayer's thermal stability or mechanical stresses that damage it may limit performance.
The intervention is targeted at temperatures up to approximately 1000°C, accident-duration transients, and extended subcritical-water exposure.
The optimal Al2O3 thickness and processing conditions are not established.
Long-term mechanical compatibility under thermal cycling and radiation remains uncertain.
